item.title: Global terrestrial biodiversity hotspots are in 'land use debt,' study finds
item.description: Global terrestrial biodiversity hotspots are among the most ecologically important regions on Earth. These 36 regions, which occupy only 2.5% of the planet's land surface, support nearly half of all plant species and more than one-third of terrestrial vertebrates.

item.title: Roads can become more dangerous on hot days – especially for pedestrians, cyclists and motorcyclists
item.description: We tend to adapt quickly to rain. But a growing body of research shows we also need to be more careful when it comes to travel and commuting during extreme heat.

item.title: A crew member’s “medical concern” foils a planned spacewalk outside the ISS
item.description: "The situation is stable," NASA said in a statement Wednesday.

item.title: Combining ecological restoration with climate-resilient agriculture to tackle desertification
item.description: Desertification threatens 24% of the world's land area spanning 126 countries and impacts 35% of the global population. Yet mainstream global efforts to tackle desertification prioritize short-term vegetation greening over addressing resource constraints and local livelihoods, creating hidden barriers to achieving the United Nations' long-term Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

item.title: Exercise may relieve depression as effectively as antidepressants
item.description: A comprehensive review confirms the benefits of exercise for treating depression, even if the exact reasons remain unclear

item.title: Ford is getting ready to put AI assistants in its cars
item.description: The Blue Oval is also working on new hands-free driver assists.

item.title: Dogs' dinners can have greater climate impact than those of their owners
item.description: Dogs fed on premium, meat-rich pet food can have a bigger dietary carbon pawprint than their owners, according to the largest study into dog food's climate impact.

item.title: Weight regain seems to occur within 2 years of stopping obesity drugs
item.description: Drugs like Ozempic have transformed how we treat obesity, but a review of almost 40 studies shows it doesn't take long for people to regain weight if they come off them

item.title: Samsung’s Ballie home robot, once promised for summer 2025, gets grim update
item.description: Six years after its CES debut, Samsung has demoted Ballie to internal use.

item.title: AI starts autonomously writing prescription refills in Utah
item.description: The program allows patients in the state to get prescription refills for 190 common meds.

item.title: Solar physicists discover long-hidden source of gamma rays unleashed by flares
item.description: Solar physicists say they have found a key source of intense gamma rays unleashed when Earth's nearest star produces its most violent eruptions.

item.title: Plasma rings around M dwarf stars offer new clues to planetary habitability
item.description: How does a star affect the makeup of its planets? And what does this mean for the habitability of distant worlds? Carnegie's Luke Bouma is exploring a new way to probe this critical question—using naturally occurring space weather stations that orbit at least 10% of M dwarf stars during their early lives. He is presenting his work at the 247th American Astronomical Society meeting.

item.title: Snow's compressibility acts as avalanche crumple zone
item.description: How do avalanches affect pylons and other sensitive infrastructure? Using detailed simulations, SLF researcher Michael Kohler has shown that the compressibility of snow initially reduces avalanche pressure, but that at high speeds this buffer suddenly fails.

item.title: Chasing ghost plumes: How underwater drones captured the secret 48-hour countdown to algal blooms
item.description: Globally, toxic algal blooms are becoming more frequent and severe, fueled by a warming climate and nutrient runoff. While satellites can easily spot the green carpets once they reach the surface, the "prequels" to these outbreaks remain hidden in the deep.

item.title: Swinging abyss: Oxygen isotope analysis shows less dynamic Antarctic ice sheet in Oligocene period
item.description: Oxygen isotopes data enable researchers to look far back into the geologic past and reconstruct the climate of the past. In doing so, they consider several factors such as ocean temperature and ice volume in polar regions. A new publication by an international team from Bergen (Norway) and Bremen in Nature Geoscience concludes that the Antarctic ice sheet was less dynamic during the Oligocene epoch 34 to 23 million years ago than previously assumed.

item.title: Warner Bros. sticks with Netflix merger, calls Paramount’s $108B bid “illusory”
item.description: Larry Ellison pledged $40B, but "he didn’t raise the price," Warner chair says.

item.title: Image: Lightning from above
item.description: NASA astronaut Nichole Ayers captured this image of lightning while orbiting aboard the International Space Station more than 250 miles above Milan, Italy on July 1, 2025.

item.title: Lunar spacecraft exhaust could obscure clues to origins of life
item.description: Over half of the exhaust methane from lunar spacecraft could end up contaminating areas of the moon that might otherwise yield clues about the origins of Earthly life, according to a recent study. The pollution could unfold rapidly regardless of a spacecraft's touchdown site; even for a landing at the South Pole, methane molecules may "hop" across the lunar surface to the North Pole in under two lunar days.

item.title: Vera C. Rubin Observatory spots record-breaking asteroid in pre-survey observations
item.description: Astronomers analyzing data from Vera C. Rubin Observatory have discovered the fastest-ever spinning asteroid with a diameter over half a kilometer—a feat uniquely enabled by Rubin. The study provides crucial information about asteroid composition and evolution, and demonstrates how Rubin is pushing the boundaries of what we can discover within our own solar system.

item.title: Sentinel-1's decade of essential data over shifting ice sheets
item.description: The extent and speed of ice moving off the ice sheets of Greenland and Antarctica into the sea—an important dynamic for climate and sea-rise modeling—has been captured over a 10-year period by satellites from the Copernicus Sentinel-1 mission.

item.title: North Pacific winter storm tracks shifting poleward much faster than predicted
item.description: Alaska's glaciers are melting at an accelerating pace, losing roughly 60 billion tons of ice each year. About 4,000 kilometers to the south, in California and Nevada, records for heat and dryness are being shattered, creating favorable conditions for wildfire events.

item.title: Hunting with poison arrows may have begun 60,000 years ago in Africa
item.description: A collection of arrow points excavated in South Africa has provided the oldest direct evidence of hunters deploying plant-based poisons on their weapons, a practice that has continued into modern times in some traditional cultures

item.title: Urban atmosphere acts as primary reservoir of microplastics, researchers find
item.description: Over the past two decades, microplastics (MPs) and nanoplastics (NPs) have been recognized as emerging pollutants, detected across every environmental compartment of Earth's system—the atmosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere, and biosphere.

item.title: Bose open-sources its SoundTouch home theater smart speakers ahead of end-of-life
item.description: If companies insist on bricking gadgets, this is a better way to do it.

item.title: Expired certificate completely breaks macOS Logitech apps, user customizations
item.description: Even with a fix available, broken apps won't be able to update themselves.

item.title: Simulation model provides accurate assessment of urban spread, residual risks of chemical warfare agents
item.description: A research team affiliated with UNIST has reported a new simulation tool to better understand how liquid-phase chemical warfare agents (CWAs) disperse and persist in urban environments. Their findings demonstrate that certain highly toxic chemical agents can remain dangerous even after initial deployment, mainly because droplets that settle on surfaces can evaporate over time and cause secondary exposure.

item.title: Marine geoscientists link warming with ancient ocean 'salty blob'
item.description: Climate change has many culprits, from agriculture to transportation to energy production. Now, add another: the deep ocean salty blob.

item.title: SteamOS continues its slow spread across the PC gaming landscape
item.description: Legion Go 2 support announced at CES, wide support for Arm hardware coming soon.

item.title: Japanese nuclear plant operator fabricated seismic risk data
item.description: Company staff were very selective about how they modeled earthquake dangers.

item.title: Sandblasting on Mars: Camera reveals how prevailing winds shape elongated landforms in volcanic zone
item.description: Martian winds can have quite an impact. ESA's Mars Express has spotted them whipping up sand grains and acting as a cosmic sandblaster, carving out intriguing grooves near Mars's equator.

item.title: Inside the massive radio search of our newest interstellar guest
item.description: It feels like every week now we're writing a new article about how 3I/ATLAS is not an alien technology. But it's worth reiterating, and perhaps taking a look at the methodology we used to prove that statement. A new paper, available in pre-print form on arXiv from Sofia Sheikh of the SETI Institute and her co-authors, details how one specific instrument—the Allen Telescope Array (ATA)—contributed to that effort.

item.title: Can recycling urine help combat the climate crisis?
item.description: In the last century, synthetic fertilizers have changed the face of the planet. The current world population might be halved if not for this useful development.

item.title: EVs remain a niche choice in the US, according to survey
item.description: Consumers around the world told Deloitte what they want in their next vehicle.

item.title: Supernova remnant video from NASA's Chandra is decades in making
item.description: A new video shows the evolution of Kepler's Supernova Remnant using data from NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory captured over more than two and a half decades.

item.title: Small-scale rainforest clearing drives majority of carbon loss, study finds
item.description: Think of the destruction of Earth's rainforests and a familiar image may come to mind: fires or chainsaws tearing through enormous swaths of the Amazon, releasing masses of planet-warming carbon dioxide.

item.title: The Milky Way's black hole is hiding an explosive past, evidence suggests
item.description: Our galaxy's supermassive black hole is famous for being one of the dimmest in the universe. Evidence from a new space telescope shows that might not always have been the case.

item.title: German emissions cuts slow, North Sea has warmest year on record
item.description: Germany's greenhouse gas emission cuts slowed sharply in 2025 as the North Sea experienced its warmest year on record, piling pressure Wednesday on the conservative-led government to boost climate protection efforts.

item.title: France halts imports of food with traces of banned pesticides
item.description: France on Wednesday officialized a ban on food imports containing traces of five pesticides currently banned in the EU, a move aimed at easing farmers' opposition to the Mercosur trade deal with four South American nations.

item.title: Stars that die off the beaten path
item.description: Astronomers have created a detailed forecast of where they expect to observe future stellar explosions in a nearby galaxy, opening a new window into how exploding stars shape the cosmos. Focusing on M33, a spiral galaxy about 2.7 million light‑years away, this research combined new maps of cold atomic hydrogen gas from the U.S. National Science Foundation Very Large Array (NSF VLA) with millimeter‑wave observations of molecular gas from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA).

item.title: New battery idea gets lots of power out of unusual sulfur chemistry
item.description: Rather than being used as a storage material, the sulfur gives up electrons.

item.title: Hominin fossils from Morocco may be close ancestors of modern humans
item.description: The jawbones and vertebrae of a hominin that lived 773,000 years ago have been found in North Africa and could represent a common ancestor of Homo sapiens, Neanderthals and Denisovans

item.title: Super-low-density worlds reveal how common planetary systems form
item.description: Most planetary systems contain worlds larger than Earth but smaller than Neptune, and the low-density planets around one young star should help us understand how such systems form

item.title: We have a fossil closer to our split with Neanderthals and Denisovans
item.description: A recent study suggests that North Africa may be a key place to look.

item.title: How rethinking your relationship with time could give you more of it
item.description: You might feel like the days and weeks are slipping by. Here is how one psychologist says you can shift your experience of time

item.title: Four baby planets show how super-Earths and sub-Neptunes form
item.description: Thanks to the discovery of thousands of exoplanets to date, we know that planets bigger than Earth but smaller than Neptune orbit most stars. Oddly, our sun lacks such a planet. That's been a source of frustration for planetary scientists, who can't study them in as much detail as they'd like, leaving one big question: How did these planets form?

item.title: Where will the next megafire break out? Climate change is making it tougher to predict
item.description: Much of south-eastern Australia is currently in the grip of a heat wave, which is expected to peak over the next two days. Heat waves often trigger bushfires, particularly if combined with strong winds.

item.title: Cyclones get names but deadly heat waves don't. Should Australia personalize severe weather?
item.description: Australia's climate is changing rapidly due to rising global greenhouse gas emissions. Extreme weather events such as tropical cyclones, east coast low pressure systems, flash floods, droughts, bushfires, severe storms, and both land and marine heat waves are becoming increasingly common, as the National Climate Risk Assessment makes clear.

item.title: Yes, forest trees die of old age. But the warming climate is killing them faster
item.description: Across Australia, forests are quietly changing. Trees that once stood for decades or centuries are now dying at an accelerating rate. And this is not because of fire, storms, or logging. The chronic stress of a warming climate is killing them.

item.title: A red moon, a blue moon, a supermoon and more: Your guide to the southern sky in 2026
item.description: What will we see in the southern sky in 2026? A total eclipse of the moon (at a convenient time), a blue moon and a supermoon, the two brightest planets close together, and Jupiter disappearing behind the moon in the daytime.

item.title: Computer scientist Yann LeCun: “Intelligence really is about learning”
item.description: The AI pioneer talks about stepping down from Meta, limits of large language models.

item.title: Dark matter and neutrinos may interact, challenging standard model of the universe
item.description: Scientists are a step closer to solving one of the universe's biggest mysteries as new research finds evidence that two of its least understood components may be interacting, offering a rare window into the darkest recesses of the cosmos.

item.title: You've heard of climate change. What is the climate debt doom loop?
item.description: Municipal bonds are a time-honored way to fund roads, schools, bridges and other public projects while paying investors interest, usually at tax-free rates.

item.title: China’s clean tech charm offensive wins Global South hearts and minds
item.description:
A new survey shows growing public willingness to buy Chinese clean technologies, write Chris Aylett and Bernice Lee

item.title: Flood literacy gaps persist as nature-based solutions prove effective against increasing water events
item.description: For decades, flooding has remained one of the most destructive and deadly natural disasters in the United States, causing an average of $8 billion in damages and nearly 90 deaths each year.

item.title: Review: Stranger Things’ frustrating finale didn’t quite stick the landing
item.description: Sure, there were many great moments, but in the end, they didn't add up to a satisfying whole.

item.title: How is drought in New England affecting water levels and the environment?
item.description: Recent reports of wells drying up in New Hampshire reflect a pattern we're increasingly seeing across New England: extended dry periods and below-normal precipitation are stressing shallow groundwater systems that many homeowners depend on.

item.title: Human-made materials could make up as much as half of some Scottish beaches
item.description: The natural sands of beaches along the Firth of Forth are being mixed with significant amounts of human-made materials like bricks, concrete, glass and industrial waste, new research has revealed.

item.title: Indian law enforcement targets climate activists accused of opposing fossil fuels
Oil residues can travel over 5,000 miles on ocean debris, study finds
item.description: When oily plastic and glass, as well as rubber, washed onto Florida beaches in 2020, a community group shared the mystery online, attracting scientists' attention. Working together, they linked the black residue-coated debris to a 2019 oil slick along Brazil's coastline. Using ocean current models and chemical analysis, the team explains in Environmental Science & Technology how some of the oily material managed to travel over 5,200 miles (8,500 kilometers) by clinging to debris.

item.title: What would Trump’s Venezuela oil plans mean for climate change?
Deploying a hybrid approach to Web3 in the AI era
item.description: When the concept of “Web 3.0” first emerged about a decade ago the idea was clear: Create a more user-controlled internet that lets you do everything you can now, except without servers or intermediaries to manage the flow of information. Where Web2, which emerged in the early 2000s, relies on centralized systems to store data…

item.title: Minerals, EVs and US tensions: what next for China and Latin America in 2026?
item.description:
Raw materials still drive relations, but China’s presence in the region is changing, with fewer loans, shifting investments and tensions with the US

The post Minerals, EVs and US tensions: what next for China and Latin America in 2026? appeared first on Dialogue Earth.

item.title: Image: Algae swirls across a South African reservoir
item.description: On clear days in Hartbeespoort, South Africa, satellite images often reveal a reservoir with shades of deep blue interrupted by drifting patches of vivid green. These shifting features indicate algae blooms, which can affect water quality, ecosystems, and nearby human communities.

item.title: The next great space race: Building data centers in orbit
item.description: Google, SpaceX and Blue Origin are reportedly racing to develop technology for AI data centers in space, but it will likely be years before we see them rocketing into the sky, experts say.

item.title: FAST J0139+4328 is a low-surface-brightness galaxy, deep imaging reveals
item.description: Astronomers from Serbia and Russia have conducted deep optical observations of a cloud of neutral atomic hydrogen, designated FAST J0139+4328. Results of the observational campaign, published December 31 on the arXiv preprint server, provide evidence that FAST J0139+4328 is a low-surface-brightness galaxy.

item.title: The Download: war in Europe, and the company that wants to cool the planet
item.description: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Europe’s drone-filled vision for the future of war Last spring, 3,000 British soldiers deployed an invisible automated intelligence network, known as a “digital targeting web,” as part of a NATO exercise called Hedgehog…

item.title: Environmentalists push back against US EPA plan to extend coal plant closings
item.description: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency is facing strong public opposition to its proposed plans to extend closure deadlines until October 2031 for 11 coal plants across the country—three of which are in Illinois and one in northwest Indiana.

item.title: Here are the launches and landings we’re most excited about in 2026
item.description: A lot could happen in space next year, but let's get real about what actually will.

item.title: LLMs contain a LOT of parameters. But what’s a parameter?
item.description: MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here. I am writing this because one of my editors woke up in the middle of the night and scribbled on a bedside notepad: “What is a…

item.title: El Nino developing rapidly, likely by summer 2026; could be strong: Experts
The man who made India digital isn’t done yet
item.description: Nandan Nilekani can’t stop trying to push India into the future. He started nearly 30 years ago, masterminding an ongoing experiment in technological state capacity that started with Aadhaar—the world’s largest digital identity system. Aadhaar means “foundation” in Hindi, and on that bedrock Nilekani and people working with him went on to build a sprawling…

item.title: AI chatbots miss urgent issues in queries about women's health
item.description: AI models such as ChatGPT and Gemini fail to give adequate advice for 60 per cent of queries relating to women’s health in a test created by medical professionals

item.title: CAR T-cell therapy makes ageing guts heal themselves
item.description: Immune cells are most commonly engineered to kill cancers, but now, scientists have shown the technique makes the gut lining of older mice resemble that of younger mice, raising hopes that the same approach could work in people

item.title: Where will the next megafire break out? Climate change is making it tougher to predict
item.description: We know that heatwaves often trigger bushfires. But predicting when and where large fires will break out is getting more difficult with a warming climate.

item.title: As Australia bakes through an extreme heatwave, even insects aren’t immune to its impact
item.description: Insects have a range of fascinating ways to keep cool. We can help them too.
